aboutAuthor: Neil Borate, Aprajita Sharma and Aditya Kondawar are financial journalists tracking Indian markets. They reconstruct Rakesh Jhunjhunwala's journey from borrowed capital to a Rs 35,000 crore portfolio with balance and primary interviews.

points.heading: Trader and investor need separate ledgers
points.body: Jhunjhunwala ran trading for cash flow with strict stops and investing for compounding with patience, never mixing the two rules. Segregating capital and mindsets let him stay long Titan through 2008 without forced selling.

points.heading: Borrowed capital at high cost demands structure
points.body: Starting with Rs 15-20 lakh at 18-24 percent when FDs paid ten percent, he survived only by monetizing currency-commodity theses and budget calls quickly enough to repay usurious interest — leverage as tool, not lifestyle.

points.heading: Titan is the template
points.body: An unorganized to organized trust shift, Tata distribution, and Tanishq purity promise turned a dismissed watch firm into a compounding machine. Seeing brand where others saw assembler and holding through flat years created outsized power-law returns.

points.heading: Credit moats are confidence
points.body: CRISIL's mandated oligopoly compounded reliably, while DHFL's short-funded long-assets collapsed when wholesale funding froze. Financial durability must be checked on liability stack, not loan growth.

points.heading: Small failures are tuition if sized small
points.body: A2Z Infra and Mandhana show that cash conversion and owned IP matter more than order books or licensed logos. Keeping them under two percent of net worth let one Titan fund dozens of errors.

points.heading: Optimism plus risk discipline, not leverage copying
points.body: Betting on India's runway works when paired with multi-year patience and trading stops isolated from core holdings. Do not mimic leverage or lifestyle habits he himself flagged as ruinous.

insights: The Sesa Goa currency-commodity math in 1986-88 that turned borrowing at 24 percent into Rs 2.5 crore before age thirty.
The Titan store-visit diligence — counting World of Titan footfalls and karat tests — behind a fifteen-year hold from Rs 30 to Rs 2,500.
The DHFL reversal where averaging a solvency event as if it were systemic panic violated his own trading versus investing segregation.
conclusion: The Big Bull of Dalal Street shows how family grounding, India optimism, and radical segregation of trading and investing let contradictory talents compound, while unflinching post-mortems on DHFL and A2Z warn what not to copy.
